issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: For a 35-year-old single male special education teacher reporting a mugging/robbery, 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on self-blame and persistent danger, but this item implies a salient role failure theme (e.g. partner/parent/protector) that is not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, or memory.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense shame and intense rage on recall can coexist, but paired with a mugging/robbery and the rest of this profile they pull toward different meanings of the event without enough support elsewhere. Shame would usually connect to strong self-blame/humiliation themes, while rage would connect to injustice/anger themes; the profile does not integrate both clearly.

vignette:
Nathan, a 35-year-old special education teacher, had always believed that his role was to create a safe and nurturing environment for his students. He took pride in his ability to connect with them, understanding their unique needs, and supporting their growth. However, his life took a sharp turn one evening during a routine trip to the grocery store, a place he had visited countless times without incident. 

As Nathan walked back to his car, he was suddenly confronted by two masked individuals demanding his wallet. The fear that surged through him was unlike anything he had experienced before. When they began shouting, the world around him faded, and all he could hear were their voices-sharp, piercing, and filled with aggression. He had felt utterly powerless, paralyzed in that moment, as they rifled through his belongings and took what little he had. Their shouts echoed in his mind long after they had disappeared into the night.

In the following weeks, Nathan's life began to unravel. The simple act of entering any building became daunting; he would instinctively scan for exits, his heart racing as he imagined potential threats lurking around every corner. It was as if the shadows whispered warnings, and he felt the weight of vigilance pressing down on him. Even in the comfort of his home, he found it nearly impossible to relax. He would sit on his couch, aware of the safe walls surrounding him, yet still unable to let go of the tension that gripped his body. The thought that he could be attacked again haunted him, leaving him in a constant state of alertness.

Memories of the mugging flooded his mind with an intensity that left him gasping for breath. Each recollection felt like a vivid photograph, seared into his consciousness. He could recall every detail-the way the streetlights flickered, the glint of a knife, the fear in his own eyes mirrored in their masks. Yet with these memories came a wave of conflicting emotions; alongside the fear, there was an intense rage at himself for being caught off guard. Nathan could not understand why he had let this happen; he often compared himself to others, convinced that someone more vigilant would have avoided the situation altogether. This self-critique gnawed at him, breeding a sense of inadequacy that tainted his interactions with colleagues and friends.

At work, Nathan struggled to maintain his composure. His students needed his support, yet he often found himself irritable and withdrawn. The constant hypervigilance made it difficult to focus on their needs; he was overwhelmed by the fear that he might fail them, just as he felt he had failed himself. The authority presence of police officers on campus triggered a visceral response in him, pulling him back to that night. Whenever he saw them, his heart raced, and his body tensed, a reminder of helplessness that he could not shake. He felt trapped in a cycle of anger and guilt, convinced that he was somehow to blame for the trauma he had endured. 

Months passed, and Nathan's social life dwindled. Friends reached out, but he turned them down, unwilling to share the inner turmoil that consumed him. Avoidance became his coping mechanism; he isolated himself, believing that staying away from situations that reminded him of the trauma would offer some solace. Yet, this only deepened his sense of loneliness, and the walls of his apartment began to close in around him.

It was during a particularly challenging day at school, when a loud argument erupted among the students, that Nathan realized he could no longer bear the weight of his experiences alone. The shouting triggered a flood of memories, and he found himself frozen, unable to respond to his students. In that moment, he understood the impact of his trauma on his life, both personally and professionally. This was not the teacher he wanted to be; he yearned to reclaim his sense of self, to reconnect with his passion for teaching.

Motivated by this realization, Nathan sought help. He hoped that therapy would provide him with the tools to process his trauma and gradually ease the burden of fear that had come to dictate his life. What frightened him most was the uncertainty of whether he could ever feel safe again, but he clung to a flicker of hope that healing was possible.
